# Global Engineering Leadership Minor
Source: https://academiccatalog.umd.edu/undergraduate/colleges-schools/engineering/global-engineering-leadership-minor/
Source: https://eng.umd.edu/global/coursework
Fetched: 2026-09-28

## Catalog requirements

The minor in Global Engineering Leadership consists of 16 credit hours. A maximum of six credits may also count toward the student's major, and no more than six credits may be taken at an institution other than the University of Maryland, College Park. All courses counted toward the minor must be completed with a "C-" or better. The following courses are required:
Course | Title | Credits
ENES317 | Introduction to Leadership in Engineering, Science, and Technology (DSSP) | 3
ENES472 | Leading Global Teams and Engaging Across Cultures in Business, Engineering, and Technology (DVCC) | 3
ENES424 | Engineering Leadership Capstone: Inclusive Leadership in Addressing Organizational & Societal Challenges | 3
ENES138 | Exploring Engineering Design Through Dialogue | 1
or WEID138 | Bridging Divides thru Intergroup Dialogue Across Disciplines
or WEID139 | Navigating Difference through Intergroup Dialogue
or CHSE328
ELECTIVE | Global Perspectives Elective | 3
ELECTIVE | Leadership Elective | 3
Total Credits | 16
Visit the website at eng.umd.edu/global/coursework for more information.

Minor in Global Engineering Leadership
Minor in Global Engineering Leadership
The engineering industry requires leadership to be exercised at all layers of an organization and today’s engineering leaders need to lead with a global vision and be knowledgeable of how to effectively lead global teams. The minor will position students to be more competitive in the job market and help students develop the skills necessary to be an effective leader and manager.
The minor in global engineering leadership is designed to develop the skills necessary to lead with a global vision, work effectively with others to address social issues, and engineer solutions that improve communities and organizations.
Students may earn the minor and a notation on their official transcript by successfully completing coursework which focuses on developing the following:
An understanding of leadership theories and current best practices for leading within engineering industry
A personal approach to leadership grounded in one’s strengths
A global perspective of leadership and an ability to effectively manage global teams and global projects
A deep understanding of cultural dimensions and an understanding of business practices and effective approaches to negotiation around the world
Organizational theories and effective practices for leading change within organizations

Alum Spotlight: Madelaine Lebetkin
Madelaine Lebetkin graduated from UMD with a Bachelor’s in Aerospace Engineering and a Minor in Global Engineering Leadership in 2023.
Q: What are you currently doing?
A: Shortly after graduation, I moved to West Texas. I work at Blue Origin in the New Shepard Program: a commercial space flight program that essentially sends everyday people, like you and me, to space for 10 minutes.
I am a launch vehicle test engineer specific to the propulsion module. I definitely work more on the maintenance side. My team is in charge of vehicle refurbishment, as well as pre- and post-launch power verifications and operations. I was part of the launch crew that sent Mihi Benhouse, the first wheelchair user who flew to space!
Q: Is there a time you recently used a lesson or skills you learned in the Minor?
A: For our final project in ENES317, we had to make an argument for one of the leadership theories we learned, and really go all in: defend it as the best leadership practice there is. I chose authentic leadership.
I think a lot about stigma and stereotypes. The only way to break those down is to be authentic to yourself. Especially in Texas…I'm working with people from wildly different backgrounds and life experiences, and who may have never been exposed to a young woman in an engineering position. Suddenly, they are being challenged on what they believe a leader looks like. Had I not gone in with the perspective of authentic leadership, I definitely would have been…shaking in my boots a little bit more.
Q: What is something you want current Minor students to know?
A: I felt it was so important to seek the Minor out, because engineers–not all, but a lot–really struggle with communication. When I'm showcasing and highlighting myself, especially to a hiring manager, I want them to know I’ve thought about that. I've spent time on my own leadership style, who I want to be, and what I want to represent when I'm in the workplace, or in front of a team as the task lead.
As an engineer, having that perspective going in–it makes for better teams.
